title: California's Worker Protection Laws Shield Employees From ICE Overreach at the Workplace
excerpt: As federal immigration enforcement intensifies, California employers face strict obligations under AB 450 and the new Workplace Know Your Rights Act to protect workers during ICE inspections.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • California's AB 450 and SB 294 protect workers from ICE overreach during inspections.
  • Employers face penalties up to $10,000 for violating employee notification laws.
  • 12% drop in noncitizen employment in California followed workplace raids.
  • New rights for employees include emergency contact designations by 2026.
  • California's laws apply to all workers, regardless of immigration status.
California's Worker Protection Laws

ICE arrested more than 43,000 people last month — a record since President Donald Trump took office — and California workplaces have increasingly found themselves on the front lines. In response, employers across the state are scrambling to understand two overlapping laws that define what they must, and must not, do when federal immigration agents show up: Assembly Bill 450, the Immigrant Worker Protection Act, and Senate Bill 294, the Workplace Know Your Rights Act.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=GwvOJbC8pik

Together, the laws create one of the most detailed employer-facing immigration compliance frameworks in the country. Getting it wrong can cost thousands of dollars per violation.

What AB 450 Requires

Signed into law in 2017, AB 450 bars employers from granting "voluntary consent" to immigration enforcement agents seeking access to nonpublic areas of a workplace or to employee records. Under Government Code Section 7285.1, agents can only enter restricted spaces — offices, break rooms, storage areas — with a valid judicial warrant signed by a judge. Administrative warrants issued by ICE, including Form I-200 (Warrant for Arrest of Alien) and Form I-205 (Warrant of Removal/Deportation), do not qualify.

The distinction matters. "Judicial warrants are issued by a federal or state judge upon a finding of probable cause and will clearly display the issuing court's name at the top," according to Buchalter, a California law firm that advises employers on immigration compliance. ICE administrative warrants, by contrast, are signed by immigration officers and carry no court authorization.

Employers who receive a Notice of Inspection of I-9 employment verification forms must notify all current employees within 72 hours, providing the name of the agency, the date the notice was received, and the nature of the inspection. After results come in, each affected employee must receive a copy of the findings and written details about any deficiencies, correction timelines, and their right to legal representation.

"Employers that violate either the access or notice provisions of the law can face civil penalties between $2,000 to $5,000 for a first violation and $5,000 to $10,000 for each subsequent violation."

— FordHarrison LLP, employment law analysis

AB 450 also prohibits employers from reverifying work authorization at times or in ways not required by federal law — a protection designed to prevent selective targeting of employees based on perceived immigration status.

SB 294 Adds New Obligations for 2026

California's Workplace Know Your Rights Act, SB 294, took effect January 1, 2026, layering additional requirements on top of AB 450. The law directed the state's Labor Commissioner to publish a template notice informing employees of their rights when interacting with law enforcement — including their right to notification of immigration inspections, protection against unfair immigration-related practices, the right to organize, and constitutional protections under the Fourth and Fifth Amendments.

Employers were required to distribute the notice to all current employees by February 1, 2026, and must deliver it to new hires at the time of onboarding. Annual redistribution is mandatory. The notice template is available in nine languages: English, Spanish, Chinese, Tagalog, Vietnamese, Korean, Hindi, Urdu, and Punjabi.

SB 294 also introduced an emergency contact designation system. By March 30, 2026, employers were required to let workers designate a person to be notified if the employee is arrested or detained during work hours. If an employee is taken into custody by ICE on the job, the employer must contact that designated person.

Penalties under SB 294 reach up to $500 per employee per day of noncompliance, capped at $10,000 per employee for emergency contact violations, according to Perkins Coie.

Heightened Stakes Amid Enforcement Surge

The compliance pressure arrives during a period of aggressive federal enforcement. Private-sector employment of noncitizens in California dropped 12 percent following workplace raids in the Los Angeles area, according to a University of California, Merced analysis. Community organizers in Los Angeles have trained roughly 9,000 businesses on responding to ICE visits, including how to identify judicial warrants, mark nonpublic areas with "Employees Only" signage, and develop response protocols.

Legal experts advise employers to appoint a trained response team, clearly designate nonpublic areas with signage and keycard access, maintain detailed records of any interactions with immigration agents, and consult legal counsel before granting access to employee records.

What Workers Should Know

Employees have the right to remain silent during an enforcement action and are not required to answer questions about their immigration status. They may refuse to sign documents without consulting an attorney and can request legal counsel before responding to any questions. Statements made to agents can be used as evidence in subsequent proceedings.

For the estimated 600,000 Indian-born residents of California — many on employment-based visas — these protections apply regardless of immigration status. AB 450 and SB 294 obligate employers to protect all workers during enforcement actions, not just those suspected of lacking authorization.
